description:
`@type list :: {atom, integer}` compiles without complaint, binds `list` in the
module namespace, and then HAS NO EFFECT: `classify_name` matches the builtin
before it ever looks at the user's declaration, so a later bare `list` resolves
to the builtin `list(any)`.

## Repro

    defmodule M do
      @type list :: {atom, integer}
      @spec f(list) :: integer
      fn f(x), do: 1
    end
    fn main() do
      dbg(M.f({:a, 2}))
    end

    error[spec/violation]: call to `f/1` violates its @spec for arguments ({:a, int})
      --> repro.fz:8:7
     8 |   dbg(M.f({:a, 2}))
       |       ^^^^^^^^^^^^ no declared @spec accepts these arguments

The user declared EXACTLY the type the argument has, and the call was rejected
against the builtin `list` instead.

## Mechanism, both halves current

- resolve.rs:390-406 `classify_name` calls `find_constructor(name)` FIRST and
  returns `NameClass::Builtin` before `reference_type` is ever reached. `list` is
  `CONSTRUCTORS[12]` at resolve.rs:120.
- source_publish.rs:1687-1695 `collect_type_refs` asks only
  `world.reference_type(scope, path, arity)`, so a user binding for a builtin
  name looks like a real `TypeDefined` reference and a real wait. Its own doc
  comment says "Builtins are not references; resolution decides them" -- but it
  has no way to tell a builtin from a user binding.
- source_publish.rs:553-582 `reserve_types` binds any `@type` name into the
  namespace with NO collision check.

So the publish-time reference walk and the resolver disagree about whether a
builtin name is taken, and the user's type is recorded as a real reference and
then never consulted.

## Elixir's answer settles the design choice

Elixir rejects the declaration outright:

    ** (Kernel.TypespecError) type list/0 is a built-in type and it cannot be redefined

So take option (b): `reserve_types` rejects a `@type` whose name collides with a
`CONSTRUCTORS` entry, as a user-facing compile error. Option (a) -- skip the ref
in `collect_type_refs` -- makes the two passes agree but leaves the declaration
silently inert, which Elixir does not do and users would not expect.

The old ticket left this as "needs investigation into which reserved-word errors
already exist for precedent". Elixir supplies the precedent; the question is
answered.

## Checks

- The repro emits a `@type` redefinition error naming `list`, at the `@type`
  line's span, and does not reach the spec-violation path.
- EVERY builtin in `CONSTRUCTORS` is covered by the same check
  (nil bool integer float cpointer binary atom any never utf8 pid ref list
  resource map), not just `list`.
- Existing user `@type` declarations on non-builtin names
  (fixtures2/00079_type_aliases_in_module.fz,
  00091_spec_resolves_local_types.fz) stay green.
- A parameterized collision (`@type list(t)` vs `list` at arity 0-1) resolves the
  same way -- `find_constructor` matches on name alone, ignoring arity.
- Full lib + matrix.

Line refs in the old ticket drifted: ~1634 -> 1687, ~526 -> 553.
title: A @type declaration silently shadows a builtin type constructor and is discarded
